<reason>Both sides were sharp and stayed on the motion. A built an excellent structural critique — opt-in is a right the powerful exercise and the powerless are quietly punished for, so non-waivable collective terms are the real instrument — and landed the best single line of pressure with the waivability dilemma and the retaliation-proof problem (casting is discretionary, unrecorded, unexplained). But B answered the dilemma directly and coherently in the required A1:/A2: format: the ban on bundling cloning consent with employment is non-waivable, while the yes itself remains individual, separately paid and project-specific. A's rejoinder ("the protective part is collective, so it's my instrument") does not dissolve that, because A's own plan permits studios to synthesize a performance the actor refused so long as it pays scale and discloses. B named that cost memorably and repeatedly — "terms without consent mean paid impersonation" — and A never offered a remedy for the identity harm beyond a label and a model-deletion rule, which B credibly rebutted ("no viewer un-hears a voice because of metadata"). B also defused A's strongest independent offense, the hostage/localization collapse, with the separability point that a refusal only reverts to the human dub that has served those markets for a century; A's hybrid-cost pivot was plausible but speculative and only bites where refusals actually occur. On the motion as written — opt-in consent versus boilerplate — A effectively argued for a world where the performer can never say no, which is the harder sell after B's coercion concession was granted. A wins style points and originality; B wins the decisive comparison.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Pressure Question Q2 (waivable or not?) forcing the fork, and B's A2 answer separating a non-waivable bundling ban from the individual yes — "your collective term sets what the yes must cost; only the person decides if yes happens." That split survived A's "that's my instrument in disguise" reply and preserved B's core distinction between priced impersonation and permission.</best_rebuttal>
